findings.issue_text: [BUG] GitHubInstallation.dispatch reads integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no fallback, raising KeyError (HTTP 500) for any Integration whose metadata lacks the 'sender' key instead of rendering the graceful error page. The re-link branch is reached exactly when an Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration — the state legacy integrations are in (installed via the GitHub webhook before this flow recorded the installer, or never linked). A user in that state completing the new OAuth step gets an unhandled 500 instead of the github-integration-failed.html dialog; the diff relies on metadata['sender'] being present but contains no code that writes it, and no migration/backfill for pre-existing integrations.

[BUG] test_installation_not_found now asserts only 'Invalid installation request.', the identical string the OAuth state-mismatch and token-exchange-failure branches return, while the not-found-specific assertion ('The GitHub installation could not be found.') was deleted — the test can no longer verify the installation-not-found behavior it is named for. The genuine not-found path (Integration.DoesNotExist -> pipeline.next_step() -> build_integration failure) produces a different message than the one asserted, so the test can only pass by exercising a different branch (e.g., the hardcoded state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05' mismatching the pipeline signature); a regression that makes the not-found path crash or succeed incorrectly ships undetected, and the pass/fail signal of this test is now coupled to a state constant that is coincidental to the scenario under test.

[ADVISORY] The OAuthLoginView failure branches — token exchange body lacking 'access_token' (including the except -> payload = {} path) and get_user_info response lacking 'login' — have no test coverage: _stub_github only stubs success responses (lines 116-127 of the test diff). A regression in the graceful-degradation behavior of these branches (e.g., an unhandled exception in the except path, or the error dialog not rendering) lands silently; every existing test in this diff stubs a successful access_token and a 'login' field, so none of the four error() return sites in OAuthLoginView other than state mismatch are exercised.

[ADVISORY] The new authorize redirect passes redirect_uri (the /extensions/github/setup/ URL) to GitHub, which enforces an exact match against the GitHub App's registered callback URL — a deployment prerequisite no code, migration, or verification step in this diff establishes. GitHub Apps configured before this change (which never needed the OAuth authorize callback) fail every new installation post-deploy with GitHub's redirect_uri mismatch error until an admin manually updates the app's callback URL / enables user authorization; self-hosted operators get this with no in-product or release-note signal, and there is no test or check in the diff confirming the registered callback matches the constructed redirect_uri.

[ADVISORY] The new branch added in this diff — Integration exists with no OrganizationIntegration but status != ACTIVE (Integration.DoesNotExist on the status-filtered re-query) — is exercised by no test in the diff. The behavior change (pending-deleted integrations now yield the generic error instead of proceeding through next_step) is unverified; a regression that drops the status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE filter would reinstall a pending-deletion integration with no failing test, and the sibling test test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete only covers the OrganizationIntegration pending-deletion branch, not this one.

[ADVISORY] The diff replaces the named constant FORWARD_INSTALL_FOR with an inline provider_id == "github" comparison and relocates the explanatory comment, a pure refactor with zero behavioral change that is not traceable to the stated security requirement. Reviewers of a security PR must audit an unrelated code-style change, and any future provider needing the same forward behavior must re-derive the pattern from inline code instead of the list constant; the change adds diff noise to a security-sensitive patch with no requirement backing it.

[ADVISORY] test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found behavior: it was rewritten to use OAuth state "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05", which does not match the pipeline signature, so the test now passes via the state-mismatch error branch in OAuthLoginView, not via any installation-lookup path. Every other test in this diff (assert_setup_flow, test_github_installed_on_another_org, test_github_user_mismatch, test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete) reuses the same deterministic signature "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3" across independent test sessions, proving the signature is stable per provider — so "ddd023..." mismatches and returns the generic error page before any installation lookup occurs; the only test covering "installation not found" now covers a different branch, and a regression in installation-not-found handling would ship undetected.

[BUG] integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError (HTTP 500) for any existing Integration whose metadata lacks a "sender" key, instead of enforcing or skipping the ownership invariant. Integrations can exist before the installation webhook that records the sender has been processed (the pipeline creates the Integration from the installation API in the Integration.DoesNotExist branch of this very function), and legacy rows created before sender was persisted; any user attempting to attach such an integration to a second organization hits a 500 instead of a 4xx error page, and the security invariant silently crashes rather than failing closed with a user-facing message.

[ADVISORY] The new required pipeline state "github_authenticated_user" is never present for pipelines initiated before this code ships, so resuming any in-flight installation after deploy compares fetch_state(...) == None against the sender login and fails. Users who started a GitHub installation before the deploy and return to finish it after the deploy get the "Invalid installation request. / We could not verify the authenticity" error page despite doing nothing wrong, and must restart the flow from scratch; the failure mode is indistinguishable from the attacker-detection case, so support cannot diagnose it.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView does not handle GitHub's OAuth error callback: when the user declines the authorize prompt GitHub redirects back with error=access_denied and no code, so the view posts a None code to the token endpoint, gets no access_token, and renders the authenticity error. A user who simply cancels the GitHub authorization screen is told "We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request" — a false security alarm that will generate support tickets and mask real tampering reports inside noise.

[ADVISORY] The error() refactor breaks gettext message extraction: the short error strings are now passed as plain keyword arguments (error_short="GitHub installation pending deletion.") and wrapped only as _(error_short) on a variable, so makemessages no longer extracts them. The pre-refactor code wrapped each literal directly (_("GitHub installation pending deletion.")), so these strings were in the translation catalog; after this diff the catalog entries go stale and every user of every locale sees the hardcoded English short error in the postMessage payload, a silent regression for all non-English deployments introduced by a refactor the security requirement did not ask for.

[BUG] The installer-identity verification is enforced only on the branch where the Integration row already exists; the `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` branch completes the install with no comparison of `github_authenticated_user` against anything. GitHub delivers the `installation` webhook asynchronously while the browser redirect back to Sentry is immediate, so on a fresh install the `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` lookup races the webhook; when it loses, the pipeline advances unverified and the exact attack this PR exists to block (attacker's installation attached to a victim org) succeeds. The security control is path-dependent instead of unconditional, and no test covers the DoesNotExist-before-webhook case.

[BUG] `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` uses direct indexing on a key that only exists for integrations whose metadata was written after this PR's sender-recording change, so pre-existing Integration rows raise KeyError and return a 500 instead of the error page. Any integration created before this deploy (or whose sender-recording webhook write never ran) that re-enters this flow — e.g. the re-install-to-another-org path exercised by test_github_installed_on_another_org, where the Integration exists, the OrganizationIntegration does not, and status is ACTIVE — crashes with KeyError inside dispatch instead of rendering github-integration-failed.html. The happy-path tests pass only because the test webhook happens to populate `sender` first; no test covers metadata without the key.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView hand-rolls the OAuth2 authorize-redirect, state check, and token-exchange sequence (the comments themselves say 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params' and 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token') instead of reusing the existing OAuth2LoginView/OAuth2CallbackView machinery, creating a second parallel OAuth implementation. Drift risk is immediate and observable in this diff: the authorize URL is built by string concatenation so `redirect_uri` is not URL-encoded, and the token exchange parses the body with parse_qsl regardless of the response content type — every future OAuth fix (encoding, scopes, error params, refresh handling) must now be applied twice, and the copy that gets missed fails only in production. Future maintainers changing the shared OAuth code get no signal that this duplicate exists.

[ADVISORY] The pipeline state contract between OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation is expressed as bare string literals ("installation_id", "github_authenticated_user") duplicated across two separate classes with no shared constant or validation. A rename or typo of a state key in one view silently yields None from fetch_state in the other: `fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` returning None makes the sender comparison fail and shows users the misleading 'We could not verify the authenticity' page rather than failing loudly, so the next change to these keys produces a debugging session instead of an error.

[ADVISORY] When the Integration exists but its status is not ACTIVE (e.g. pending deletion at the Integration level after its OrganizationIntegration rows were already removed), the new `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` lookup falls into the generic `error()` path, reporting 'could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' for what is actually a mid-deletion state. A user retrying during the very 15-minute deletion window that ERR_INTEGRATION_PENDING_DELETION itself tells them to wait out now receives the wrong diagnostic ('restart the installation process'), sending them into a futile restart loop or a support ticket; the pending-deletion messaging that exists for exactly this situation is unreachable on this sub-path.

[BUG] The sender-equality check silently tightens the installation requirement from 'an authorized org member completes the Sentry setup' to 'the person completing Sentry setup must be the exact GitHub user who installed the GitHub App', a stricter constraint than the anti-hijack objective requires. A legitimate org admin who asks a colleague or owner to install the GitHub App on GitHub and then completes the Sentry integration themselves is now permanently blocked with 'Invalid installation request.' — a working flow in the pre-diff code now fails for the exact users the feature is meant to serve; no explicit acceptance of this collateral behavior change appears in the diff or tests.

[BUG] The new second lookup restricted to status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE changes behavior for non-ACTIVE integrations that have no OrganizationIntegration row: the old code bound installation_id and called pipeline.next_step(), the new code returns the generic error page. Re-linking an integration whose row exists in a disabled or pending-deletion state (e.g., after org-integration removal) to an organization previously succeeded and could reactivate it; it now hard-fails with 'Invalid installation request.' — an unannounced behavioral change beyond the stated security objective.

[BUG] The call to get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is not wrapped in any error handling, unlike the token-exchange block directly above it which catches Exception. A network failure, timeout, or non-JSON response from https://github.com/user during the install flow raises an unhandled exception, surfacing a 500 page to the user mid-install instead of the github-integration-failed.html template every other failure branch in this view returns.

[BUG] integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError (or TypeError if metadata['sender'] is not a dict) for any Integration whose stored metadata lacks a 'sender' key, a structure not guaranteed for integrations created before this metadata field was recorded. On upgraded self-hosted installs, a user re-linking a pre-existing integration whose metadata predates sender recording hits a 500 during setup instead of the error template, with no code path in this diff to handle or migrate that shape.

[ADVISORY] The specific user-facing message 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' was silently replaced by the generic 'Invalid installation request.' for the not-found case, as evidenced by the changed assertion in test_installation_not_found. Users whose installation id simply does not exist (typos, deleted apps) are told 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request', misdiagnosing a mundane configuration problem as a security failure and making support triage harder; the distinct error semantics were lost as a side effect of the refactor without an explicit decision.

[ADVISORY] The state-mismatch branch of OAuthLoginView — the check that guards the OAuth CSRF boundary of the new mandatory login step — is the only new failure path in this diff with no test driving it. A future regression that weakens or removes the pipeline.signature comparison (e.g., a refactor to the signature mechanism) would fail open, allowing a GitHub authorize callback with an attacker-chosen state to proceed to token exchange, and no test in this diff or the existing suite would catch it.

[BUG] test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found behavior: its callback request uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which differs from the pipeline signature ('9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3') that every other test in this file uses, so the request exits at the state-mismatch check in OAuthLoginView and the test asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error instead of the not-found path. The Integration.DoesNotExist branch in GitHubInstallation.dispatch (external_id lookup raising DoesNotExist -> pipeline.next_step()) and the pipeline-finish 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' behavior that this test previously verified are now covered by nothing; a regression that breaks installation-not-found handling (e.g., the lookup or the next_step advance) keeps this test green because it passes on the state-rejection error page regardless. The test name and its assertion now describe different code paths.

[ADVISORY] The new branch `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` -> DoesNotExist -> error(request, ...) has no test coverage in this diff. An operator with a soft-deleted/non-ACTIVE GitHub Integration row hits this brand-new rejection path on every install attempt; a regression here (e.g., wrong status filter that also rejects ACTIVE integrations) would block all installs, and no test in the diff would catch it. Evidence of absence: the only test file changed is tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py, and none of its tests (assert_setup_flow, test_github_installed_on_another_org, test_installation_not_found, test_github_user_mismatch, test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete) constructs an Integration with a status other than ACTIVE or otherwise triggers this branch.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView's two failure branches — token exchange yielding no 'access_token' (the try/except around safe_urlread/parse_qsl plus the `if "access_token" not in payload` guard) and get_user_info returning no 'login' — are exercised by no test in this diff; every stub added in _stub_github returns a success payload. When GitHub rate-limits or errors during the new mandatory OAuth step, real users get the generic failure dialog; a regression in the exception swallowing (e.g., the except clause masking a programming error) or in the parse_qsl handling of a non-form-encoded error body ships silently. Evidence of absence: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py is the only test file in the diff; its only stubs for https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token and /user (added at lines ~116-124) return a valid token and login, and no test registers a failing response for either endpoint.

[ADVISORY] test_github_user_mismatch (and the other new failure-path assertions in this diff) assert only the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, which error() emits identically for five distinct failure causes: state mismatch, missing access_token, missing login, inactive integration, and sender mismatch. The test pins fail-vs-success but not which guard fired: if a future change makes a different check reject the request (e.g., the state comparison or the /user call) while the sender-mismatch check itself regresses, this test still passes with the same assertion output. An author rebuttal ('assertTemplateUsed pins the failure branch') fails because all five branches render the same template and message, so the assertion cannot discriminate between them.

[ADVISORY] GitHubInstallation now hard-requires the pipeline state key 'github_authenticated_user', which is only ever written by the new OAuthLoginView, so pipelines started before this code deploys fail irrecoverably after deploy (rolling-deploy skew on pipeline state, analogous to reading a new column before backfill). A user who begins a GitHub integration install on an old pod (where get_pipeline_views returns only GitHubInstallation, so 'github_authenticated_user' is never bound) and completes it after the rolling deploy finishes hits `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with the left side None; the comparison fails and they get the 'Invalid installation request' error page with no path forward except restarting the pipeline. During a multi-hour rolling deploy this breaks any install in flight across the deploy boundary.

[BUG] The token-exchange call `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` sits outside the try/except that guards only the read/parse, so a network failure or a non-2xx GitHub response (urllib raises HTTPError) propagates out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch as an unhandled 500. A user whose GitHub token exchange hits a GitHub outage or any HTTP error gets a raw 500 mid-pipeline instead of the friendly 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request.' page that every sibling failure branch in the same method renders; the author clearly intended this path to be handled (the try block exists) but only wrapped half of it.

[BUG] `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload['access_token'])` is an unguarded outbound HTTP call inside dispatch — any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from the GitHub /user endpoint raises out of the view as a 500. A transient GitHub failure during the /user lookup turns a recoverable condition into a raw 500 that aborts the pipeline, where the surrounding code establishes the contract that all OAuth-stage failures render the github-integration-failed.html error page.

[BUG] `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` is an unguarded dict-chain access: any pre-existing GitHub integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key (integrations created before sender was recorded by the webhook, or where the installation webhook was dropped) raises KeyError. The re-install path (Integration exists, OrganizationIntegration does not) — which is exactly the population of older integrations this check targets — 500s with KeyError instead of rendering the error page or proceeding; every legacy-integration reinstall attempt fails with a 500 until the metadata is manually repaired.

[BUG] When no Integration row exists for the installation_id (including the case where the installation webhook that persists metadata['sender'] has not been processed yet), `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` skips the new authenticated-user check entirely and proceeds with the install. The sender-mismatch verification this PR introduces is only enforced when a webhook has already created the Integration row; because GitHub delivers the webhook asynchronously while redirecting the user back immediately, the same install nondeterministically either runs the check or silently skips it — a fresh install that races ahead of the webhook completes with no ownership verification and no log.

[ADVISORY] `except Exception: payload = {}` swallows every token-exchange read/parse failure — network errors, HTML error bodies, encoding failures — with no log, metric, or capture. When users report failed GitHub installs (they all see the same 'We could not verify the authenticity' page), operators have zero server-side signal to distinguish a GitHub outage from a parsing bug or a config problem; a one-line metrics/logging call before the fallback preserves the UX without blinding debugging.

[ADVISORY] The new branch fetching `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and rendering the generic error on DoesNotExist is non-trivial new logic added by this diff with no test exercising it. A regression that flips this branch back to `next_step()` (or swaps the error for success) would let integrations in non-ACTIVE states (e.g. pending deletion in another org, disabled) be silently re-installed, and nothing in the diff's test suite would catch it.

[ADVISORY] The identity check compares the mutable GitHub `login` string rather than the immutable sender account id from the webhook payload. A user who renames their GitHub account between installing the app and reinstalling/linking to another Sentry org fails the check with the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error despite being the legitimate installer; the webhook payload already carries sender.id, so keying on it removes the failure mode without extra calls.

adjudication.rationale: Diff adds new failure-return branches in OAuthLoginView: (1) token exchange parsing failure / missing "access_token" (try/except around safe_urlread+parse_qsl, then `if "access_token" not in payload: return error(...)`), and (2) `get_user_info(...)` missing "login" (`if "login" not in authenticated_user_info: return error(...)`). The updated tests’ `_stub_github()` only stubs a successful POST to `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` returning `access_token=...` and a successful GET `/user` returning `{ "login": "octocat" }`, so those error branches are never exercised. The only OAuthLoginView error path covered is the state-mismatch case (e.g., `test_installation_not_found` hits `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature: return error(...)`).

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces an OAuth authorize redirect that explicitly includes a `redirect_uri` built as `absolute_uri(reverse("sentry-extension-setup", ...))` (OAuthLoginView.dispatch). That creates an external configuration dependency: the GitHub app/OAuth configuration must accept that exact callback URL. The diff does not add any runtime validation, fallback, migration, or admin/operator-facing check to ensure the configured callback matches the constructed `redirect_uri`, so deployments with mismatched GitHub settings could see installation failures post-deploy. This is a concrete, diff-grounded operational/release concern rather than an intrinsic code defect that can be proven solely from the diff.

The finding’s complaint is primarily about diff noise/style/process (unrelated refactor in a security PR) and speculative future extensibility, not a concrete defect or a specific, diff-grounded functional/architectural problem.

Every other test in this diff (assert_setup_flow, test_github_installed_on_another_org, test_github_user_mismatch, test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete) reuses the same deterministic signature "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3" across independent test sessions, proving the signature is stable per provider — so "ddd023..." mismatches and returns the generic error page before any installation lookup occurs; the only test covering "installation not found" now covers a different branch, and a regression in installation-not-found handling would ship undetected.

adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate notes that OAuth state is derived from a deterministic, stable pipeline signature reused across sessions/tests, leading to state-mismatch behavior when it differs. This aligns with the golden issue that the OAuth state is static (pipeline.signature-based) rather than a per-request random value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError (HTTP 500) for any existing Integration whose metadata lacks a "sender" key, instead of enforcing or skipping the ownership invariant. Integrations can exist before the installation webhook that records the sender has been processed (the pipeline creates the Integration from the installation API in the Integration.DoesNotExist branch of this very function), and legacy rows created before sender was persisted; any user attempting to attach such an integration to a second organization hits a 500 instead of a 4xx error page, and the security invariant silently crashes rather than failing closed with a user-facing message.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, after fetching an existing active `Integration`, the new ownership check directly indexes `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. If `metadata` lacks `sender` (or `login`), this will raise `KeyError` and produce a 500 instead of returning the intended error page. The diff does not enforce/populate `sender` for all existing Integrations, and it explicitly targets the case where an Integration exists but is not yet linked to an org, which plausibly includes legacy or pre-webhook rows.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new required pipeline state "github_authenticated_user" is never present for pipelines initiated before this code ships, so resuming any in-flight installation after deploy compares fetch_state(...) == None against the sender login and fails. Users who started a GitHub installation before the deploy and return to finish it after the deploy get the "Invalid installation request. / We could not verify the authenticity" error page despite doing nothing wrong, and must restart the flow from scratch; the failure mode is indistinguishable from the attacker-detection case, so support cannot diagnose it.

[ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView does not handle GitHub's OAuth error callback: when the user declines the authorize prompt GitHub redirects back with error=access_denied and no code, so the view posts a None code to the token endpoint, gets no access_token, and renders the authenticity error. A user who simply cancels the GitHub authorization screen is told "We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request" — a false security alarm that will generate support tickets and mask real tampering reports inside noise.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, after the authorize redirect it unconditionally builds token-exchange `data` with `"code": request.GET.get("code")` and calls `safe_urlopen(...)` without checking for GitHub’s OAuth error callback parameters (e.g. `error=access_denied`) or even verifying `code` is present. If the user declines authorization, `code` will be missing, the access token exchange will fail (no `access_token` in `payload`), and the view renders `ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST` via `error(...)`, incorrectly implying an authenticity/tampering issue. This misleading behavior is directly introduced by the new OAuthLoginView logic in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The error() refactor breaks gettext message extraction: the short error strings are now passed as plain keyword arguments (error_short="GitHub installation pending deletion.") and wrapped only as _(error_short) on a variable, so makemessages no longer extracts them. The pre-refactor code wrapped each literal directly (_("GitHub installation pending deletion.")), so these strings were in the translation catalog; after this diff the catalog entries go stale and every user of every locale sees the hardcoded English short error in the postMessage payload, a silent regression for all non-English deployments introduced by a refactor the security requirement did not ask for.

adjudication.rationale: In the refactor, `error()` wraps `error_short` via `_(error_short)`, but call sites now pass plain string literals like `error_short="GitHub installation pending deletion."` and `error_short="Github installed on another Sentry organization."` without wrapping them in `_()`. Django’s `makemessages` typically only extracts strings used in translation function calls (e.g. `_('...')`), so these literals are no longer discoverable for the translation catalog, unlike the pre-refactor code which directly used `_('...')` in the render context. This can silently regress localized postMessage payloads to English.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The installer-identity verification is enforced only on the branch where the Integration row already exists; the `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` branch completes the install with no comparison of `github_authenticated_user` against anything. GitHub delivers the `installation` webhook asynchronously while the browser redirect back to Sentry is immediate, so on a fresh install the `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` lookup races the webhook; when it loses, the pipeline advances unverified and the exact attack this PR exists to block (attacker's installation attached to a victim org) succeeds. The security control is path-dependent instead of unconditional, and no test covers the DoesNotExist-before-webhook case.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, installer identity is only checked after an active `Integration` row is fetched (`integration = Integration.objects.get(...status=ACTIVE)` followed by comparing `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` to `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`). However, the earlier lookup `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` is wrapped in a try/except used to determine `installations_exist`, and on `except Integration.DoesNotExist:` the code immediately `return pipeline.next_step()` with no verification at all. This creates a path where a request with an `installation_id` can advance the pipeline without the new identity control being enforced (and there is no test in the diff covering this DoesNotExist path).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` uses direct indexing on a key that only exists for integrations whose metadata was written after this PR's sender-recording change, so pre-existing Integration rows raise KeyError and return a 500 instead of the error page. Any integration created before this deploy (or whose sender-recording webhook write never ran) that re-enters this flow — e.g. the re-install-to-another-org path exercised by test_github_installed_on_another_org, where the Integration exists, the OrganizationIntegration does not, and status is ACTIVE — crashes with KeyError inside dispatch instead of rendering github-integration-failed.html. The happy-path tests pass only because the test webhook happens to populate `sender` first; no test covers metadata without the key.
matched_golden_ids: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. The candidate describes that `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is accessed via direct indexing without ensuring the `sender` key exists, leading to a KeyError for pre-existing integrations or cases where sender metadata was never written. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView hand-rolls the OAuth2 authorize-redirect, state check, and token-exchange sequence (the comments themselves say 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params' and 'similar to OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token') instead of reusing the existing OAuth2LoginView/OAuth2CallbackView machinery, creating a second parallel OAuth implementation. Drift risk is immediate and observable in this diff: the authorize URL is built by string concatenation so `redirect_uri` is not URL-encoded, and the token exchange parses the body with parse_qsl regardless of the response content type — every future OAuth fix (encoding, scopes, error params, refresh handling) must now be applied twice, and the copy that gets missed fails only in production. Future maintainers changing the shared OAuth code get no signal that this duplicate exists.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OAuthLoginView` that manually implements the GitHub OAuth flow (constructing the authorize URL via string concatenation, checking `state` against `pipeline.signature`, POSTing to the access-token endpoint, and parsing with `parse_qsl`) rather than reusing existing shared OAuth2 views/helpers. This creates a parallel OAuth implementation in `src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py` that future OAuth fixes (encoding, error handling, scopes, etc.) would need to be applied to separately, increasing drift/maintenance risk. The specific implementation choices called out (string-built query, unconditional `parse_qsl` parsing) are directly observable in the new code, but they are not conclusively a current functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The pipeline state contract between OAuthLoginView and GitHubInstallation is expressed as bare string literals ("installation_id", "github_authenticated_user") duplicated across two separate classes with no shared constant or validation. A rename or typo of a state key in one view silently yields None from fetch_state in the other: `fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` returning None makes the sender comparison fail and shows users the misleading 'We could not verify the authenticity' page rather than failing loudly, so the next change to these keys produces a debugging session instead of an error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows duplicated, unvalidated pipeline state keys used across classes: `OAuthLoginView` does `pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", ...)` and `pipeline.bind_state("github_authenticated_user", ...)`, while `GitHubInstallation` reads via `pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id")` and `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")`. There is no shared constant or guard ensuring these keys exist/are consistent. If a future change introduces a typo/rename in one place, `fetch_state(...)` will return `None` and the user mismatch check will fall into the generic `error(...)` path, making debugging harder. This is a maintainability/contract-robustness concern created/exposed by the change, not a currently verifiable runtime defect in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When the Integration exists but its status is not ACTIVE (e.g. pending deletion at the Integration level after its OrganizationIntegration rows were already removed), the new `status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE` lookup falls into the generic `error()` path, reporting 'could not verify the authenticity of the installation request' for what is actually a mid-deletion state. A user retrying during the very 15-minute deletion window that ERR_INTEGRATION_PENDING_DELETION itself tells them to wait out now receives the wrong diagnostic ('restart the installation process'), sending them into a futile restart loop or a support ticket; the pending-deletion messaging that exists for exactly this situation is unreachable on this sub-path.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when an `Integration` exists but is not `ObjectStatus.ACTIVE`, the code now does `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and on `DoesNotExist` immediately returns the generic `error()` ("Invalid installation request" / authenticity failure). The only pending-deletion specific messaging (`ERR_INTEGRATION_PENDING_DELETION`) is gated earlier by an `OrganizationIntegration` query (`status=PENDING_DELETION`). So if the Integration is mid-deletion (non-ACTIVE) without a corresponding `OrganizationIntegration` row in PENDING_DELETION, this path will show the wrong diagnostic, making the intended pending-deletion guidance unreachable for that state.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The sender-equality check silently tightens the installation requirement from 'an authorized org member completes the Sentry setup' to 'the person completing Sentry setup must be the exact GitHub user who installed the GitHub App', a stricter constraint than the anti-hijack objective requires. A legitimate org admin who asks a colleague or owner to install the GitHub App on GitHub and then completes the Sentry integration themselves is now permanently blocked with 'Invalid installation request.' — a working flow in the pre-diff code now fails for the exact users the feature is meant to serve; no explicit acceptance of this collateral behavior change appears in the diff or tests.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly adds a new constraint in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`: it now rejects setup unless `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") == integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` (returning `error(...)` -> "Invalid installation request."). This indeed blocks the previously-possible flow where one GitHub user installs the GitHub App (webhook `sender`) and a different authorized Sentry/org member completes the Sentry setup. However, the change appears intentional and is codified by a new test (`test_github_user_mismatch`) asserting that this mismatch should fail, so it’s not a “silent” bug so much as a potentially impactful product/UX policy change that merits explicit acceptance/communication.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new second lookup restricted to status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE changes behavior for non-ACTIVE integrations that have no OrganizationIntegration row: the old code bound installation_id and called pipeline.next_step(), the new code returns the generic error page. Re-linking an integration whose row exists in a disabled or pending-deletion state (e.g., after org-integration removal) to an organization previously succeeded and could reactivate it; it now hard-fails with 'Invalid installation request.' — an unannounced behavioral change beyond the stated security objective.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce the stated behavior change: in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, after confirming `OrganizationIntegration` doesn’t exist for the `installation_id`, the code now does `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and returns `error(...)` if not found. Previously, in that same path it unconditionally `pipeline.bind_state(...); return pipeline.next_step()` (no status filter). This means non-ACTIVE integrations with no `OrganizationIntegration` row will now hard-fail. However, whether this is a *defect* vs an intentional tightening (given the new authenticity/user check relies on an existing, active Integration’s metadata) isn’t provable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The call to get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is not wrapped in any error handling, unlike the token-exchange block directly above it which catches Exception. A network failure, timeout, or non-JSON response from https://github.com/user during the install flow raises an unhandled exception, surfacing a 500 page to the user mid-install instead of the github-integration-failed.html template every other failure branch in this view returns.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the token-response parsing is wrapped in `try/except`, but the subsequent `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` call has no local error handling before its result is used. The diff shows this call is on the happy path and any exception from `get_user_info` would bypass the view’s `error(...)` rendering branches. However, the diff does not show `get_user_info`’s implementation, so it’s not verifiable from the PR alone that it can raise on network/parse failures (it may handle errors internally).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError (or TypeError if metadata['sender'] is not a dict) for any Integration whose stored metadata lacks a 'sender' key, a structure not guaranteed for integrations created before this metadata field was recorded. On upgraded self-hosted installs, a user re-linking a pre-existing integration whose metadata predates sender recording hits a 500 during setup instead of the error template, with no code path in this diff to handle or migrate that shape.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, after loading an existing active `Integration` (`Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)`), the code unconditionally evaluates `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` to compare against `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")`. There is no guard/`try` around missing keys or non-dict shapes, so any Integration row whose `metadata` lacks `sender` (or where `sender` is not a dict) will raise `KeyError`/`TypeError` and result in a 500 rather than the `error(...)` template. The diff adds this new access without any migration/compat handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The specific user-facing message 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' was silently replaced by the generic 'Invalid installation request.' for the not-found case, as evidenced by the changed assertion in test_installation_not_found. Users whose installation id simply does not exist (typos, deleted apps) are told 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request', misdiagnosing a mundane configuration problem as a security failure and making support triage harder; the distinct error semantics were lost as a side effect of the refactor without an explicit decision.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show a user-facing messaging change for the not-found path: `test_installation_not_found` switched from asserting `"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to asserting `"Invalid installation request."`. In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` raises `Integration.DoesNotExist`, it now returns the generic `error(...)` defaulting to `error_short="Invalid installation request."` / `ERR_INTEGRATION_INVALID_INSTALLATION_REQUEST` (“could not verify authenticity...”). This is a real, diff-grounded semantic/message regression concern, but it’s not clearly a functional correctness defect from the diff alone (it could be an intentional security/privacy choice), so it fits a non-bug review issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The state-mismatch branch of OAuthLoginView — the check that guards the OAuth CSRF boundary of the new mandatory login step — is the only new failure path in this diff with no test driving it. A future regression that weakens or removes the pipeline.signature comparison (e.g., a refactor to the signature mechanism) would fail open, allowing a GitHub authorize callback with an attacker-chosen state to proceed to token exchange, and no test in this diff or the existing suite would catch it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff *does* add test coverage for the OAuth `state` mismatch failure path. In `test_installation_not_found`, after initiating the setup flow, it performs a callback GET to `self.setup_path` with `code=...` and a deliberately different `state` (`ddd023d8...`) and asserts the response contains `"Invalid installation request."`. That request would hit `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`’s branch `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature: return error(...)`, exercising the CSRF-guarded state comparison.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the installation-not-found behavior: its callback request uses state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which differs from the pipeline signature ('9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3') that every other test in this file uses, so the request exits at the state-mismatch check in OAuthLoginView and the test asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error instead of the not-found path. The Integration.DoesNotExist branch in GitHubInstallation.dispatch (external_id lookup raising DoesNotExist -> pipeline.next_step()) and the pipeline-finish 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' behavior that this test previously verified are now covered by nothing; a regression that breaks installation-not-found handling (e.g., the lookup or the next_step advance) keeps this test green because it passes on the state-rejection error page regardless. The test name and its assertion now describe different code paths.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `test_installation_not_found` was changed to make an OAuth callback request with a different `state` (`ddd023...`) and now asserts the generic "Invalid installation request." message. In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, a `state` mismatch returns `error(...)` immediately, so this test no longer reaches `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` nor any downstream "installation not found" behavior it previously asserted (it no longer checks for "The GitHub installation could not be found."). This is a real, diff-grounded test coverage/intent mismatch (test name vs exercised path), not a confirmed production defect in the integration logic itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new branch `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` -> DoesNotExist -> error(request, ...) has no test coverage in this diff. An operator with a soft-deleted/non-ACTIVE GitHub Integration row hits this brand-new rejection path on every install attempt; a regression here (e.g., wrong status filter that also rejects ACTIVE integrations) would block all installs, and no test in the diff would catch it. Evidence of absence: the only test file changed is tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py, and none of its tests (assert_setup_flow, test_github_installed_on_another_org, test_installation_not_found, test_github_user_mismatch, test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete) constructs an Integration with a status other than ACTIVE or otherwise triggers this branch.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new rejection path in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`: it now requires `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and returns `error(...)` on `Integration.DoesNotExist` (i.e., when an Integration exists but is not ACTIVE). In the modified test file (`tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py`), the updated/added tests cover OAuth state validation and a GitHub user mismatch, but none constructs an `Integration` with `status != ACTIVE` to exercise this new branch, so regressions in the status filter or behavior would not be caught by tests in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OAuthLoginView's two failure branches — token exchange yielding no 'access_token' (the try/except around safe_urlread/parse_qsl plus the `if "access_token" not in payload` guard) and get_user_info returning no 'login' — are exercised by no test in this diff; every stub added in _stub_github returns a success payload. When GitHub rate-limits or errors during the new mandatory OAuth step, real users get the generic failure dialog; a regression in the exception swallowing (e.g., the except clause masking a programming error) or in the parse_qsl handling of a non-form-encoded error body ships silently. Evidence of absence: tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py is the only test file in the diff; its only stubs for https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token and /user (added at lines ~116-124) return a valid token and login, and no test registers a failing response for either endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new mandatory OAuthLoginView step with explicit failure branches: (1) token exchange parsing/reading failure leading to `payload = {}` and `if "access_token" not in payload: return error(...)`, and (2) `get_user_info(...)` missing a `login` leading to `return error(...)`. In the updated tests, `_stub_github()` always stubs `https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token` with `body="access_token=..."` and `/user` with `json={"login": "octocat"}`, and no test registers a non-form/non-200/error body for the token endpoint or a `/user` response lacking `login`. The new failure paths therefore are not exercised by any test in this diff, even though they represent nontrivial new behavior introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_github_user_mismatch (and the other new failure-path assertions in this diff) assert only the generic 'Invalid installation request.' message, which error() emits identically for five distinct failure causes: state mismatch, missing access_token, missing login, inactive integration, and sender mismatch. The test pins fail-vs-success but not which guard fired: if a future change makes a different check reject the request (e.g., the state comparison or the /user call) while the sender-mismatch check itself regresses, this test still passes with the same assertion output. An author rebuttal ('assertTemplateUsed pins the failure branch') fails because all five branches render the same template and message, so the assertion cannot discriminate between them.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `error()` defaults to `error_short="Invalid installation request."` and is used unchanged for multiple distinct rejection paths in `OAuthLoginView.dispatch` (state mismatch, missing `access_token`, missing `login`) and in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch` (inactive/nonexistent active integration, authenticated user mismatch). The new tests (e.g. `test_github_user_mismatch`, updated `test_installation_not_found`) assert only the generic "Invalid installation request." and the same failure template, which cannot distinguish which guard triggered. This is a specific test-coverage/precision issue created by the change, not a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] GitHubInstallation now hard-requires the pipeline state key 'github_authenticated_user', which is only ever written by the new OAuthLoginView, so pipelines started before this code deploys fail irrecoverably after deploy (rolling-deploy skew on pipeline state, analogous to reading a new column before backfill). A user who begins a GitHub integration install on an old pod (where get_pipeline_views returns only GitHubInstallation, so 'github_authenticated_user' is never bound) and completes it after the rolling deploy finishes hits `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` with the left side None; the comparison fails and they get the 'Invalid installation request' error page with no path forward except restarting the pipeline. During a multi-hour rolling deploy this breaks any install in flight across the deploy boundary.

adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate highlights that the code now assumes the pipeline state key `github_authenticated_user` exists, but it may be missing (e.g., during rolling deploys), leading to `None` being read and subsequent failure. This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment: missing `github_authenticated_user` state causing null/None-related failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The token-exchange call `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` sits outside the try/except that guards only the read/parse, so a network failure or a non-2xx GitHub response (urllib raises HTTPError) propagates out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch as an unhandled 500. A user whose GitHub token exchange hits a GitHub outage or any HTTP error gets a raw 500 mid-pipeline instead of the friendly 'We could not verify the authenticity of the installation request.' page that every sibling failure branch in the same method renders; the author clearly intended this path to be handled (the try block exists) but only wrapped half of it.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the token exchange request is made via `req = safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` **before** the `try/except` that only wraps `safe_urlread(req)` + decode/parse. If `safe_urlopen(...)` raises (e.g., network error/timeout/HTTP error), it will bypass the method’s friendly `error(...)` handling and propagate as an unhandled exception (500). The surrounding logic shows intent to convert failures into the rendered `github-integration-failed.html` page, but this call is not covered.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload['access_token'])` is an unguarded outbound HTTP call inside dispatch — any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from the GitHub /user endpoint raises out of the view as a 500. A transient GitHub failure during the /user lookup turns a recoverable condition into a raw 500 that aborts the pipeline, where the surrounding code establishes the contract that all OAuth-stage failures render the github-integration-failed.html error page.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, the code calls `authenticated_user_info = get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` without any try/except or error handling (unlike later checks that route to `error(...)`). If `get_user_info` performs an outbound HTTP request (as implied by its purpose and the test stubbing of `GET .../user`) and that request raises (timeout/connection error/non-2xx raising), the exception would propagate out of the view and result in a 500 rather than rendering `github-integration-failed.html` via `error(...)`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` is an unguarded dict-chain access: any pre-existing GitHub integration whose metadata lacks a 'sender' key (integrations created before sender was recorded by the webhook, or where the installation webhook was dropped) raises KeyError. The re-install path (Integration exists, OrganizationIntegration does not) — which is exactly the population of older integrations this check targets — 500s with KeyError instead of rendering the error page or proceeding; every legacy-integration reinstall attempt fails with a 500 until the metadata is manually repaired.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the new re-installation verification does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` without guarding for missing keys. If an existing `Integration` record has `metadata` without a `sender` (or without `login` under `sender`), this will raise `KeyError` and 500, bypassing the intended `error(...)` rendering. The diff adds no try/except around that dict-chain access.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When no Integration row exists for the installation_id (including the case where the installation webhook that persists metadata['sender'] has not been processed yet), `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` skips the new authenticated-user check entirely and proceeds with the install. The sender-mismatch verification this PR introduces is only enforced when a webhook has already created the Integration row; because GitHub delivers the webhook asynchronously while redirecting the user back immediately, the same install nondeterministically either runs the check or silently skips it — a fresh install that races ahead of the webhook completes with no ownership verification and no log.

adjudication.rationale: In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, the authenticated-user verification is only performed in the branch where an active `Integration` row exists (`integration = Integration.objects.get(...); ... pipeline.fetch_state('github_authenticated_user') != integration.metadata['sender']['login']`). But earlier, the code still does `except Integration.DoesNotExist: return pipeline.next_step()` when `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` fails, which skips the new ownership check entirely and proceeds to the next pipeline step. Since `integration.metadata['sender']` appears to come from the webhook (as implied by the new test that posts an installation webhook to set `sender.login`), a fresh install racing ahead of webhook persistence will hit this `DoesNotExist` path and bypass the check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] `except Exception: payload = {}` swallows every token-exchange read/parse failure — network errors, HTML error bodies, encoding failures — with no log, metric, or capture. When users report failed GitHub installs (they all see the same 'We could not verify the authenticity' page), operators have zero server-side signal to distinguish a GitHub outage from a parsing bug or a config problem; a one-line metrics/logging call before the fallback preserves the UX without blinding debugging.

adjudication.rationale: In `OAuthLoginView.dispatch`, token exchange response parsing is wrapped in `try: ... except Exception: payload = {}` (reading/decoding via `safe_urlread(req).decode(...)` and `parse_qsl`). The except block drops all error detail and then returns the generic `error(...)` page when `access_token` is missing, with no logging/metrics/capture shown anywhere in the diff. This is a concrete, diff-grounded observability/operability concern (hard to diagnose outages vs parsing/config issues) rather than a directly verifiable functional defect, since the fallback behavior is intentional.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new branch fetching `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and rendering the generic error on DoesNotExist is non-trivial new logic added by this diff with no test exercising it. A regression that flips this branch back to `next_step()` (or swaps the error for success) would let integrations in non-ACTIVE states (e.g. pending deletion in another org, disabled) be silently re-installed, and nothing in the diff's test suite would catch it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new non-trivial behavior in `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`: it now requires `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` and returns the generic `error(...)` on `Integration.DoesNotExist` (including the case where an Integration exists but is not ACTIVE). The updated tests cover other new branches (OAuth state mismatch -> "Invalid installation request", pending deletion error, github user mismatch, and "installed on another org"), but none exercise the specific new ACTIVE-status gate / DoesNotExist error path for a non-ACTIVE integration. So the finding about missing test coverage for this branch is grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The identity check compares the mutable GitHub `login` string rather than the immutable sender account id from the webhook payload. A user who renames their GitHub account between installing the app and reinstalling/linking to another Sentry org fails the check with the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error despite being the legitimate installer; the webhook payload already carries sender.id, so keying on it removes the failure mode without extra calls.

adjudication.rationale: The new authenticity check keys on GitHub username strings: OAuthLoginView stores `authenticated_user_info["login"]` in `github_authenticated_user`, and GitHubInstallation compares it against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. Since `login` is a mutable identifier (users can rename accounts), this can wrongly reject a legitimate installer if their username changes between the webhook-populated metadata and the OAuth login, resulting in the generic `Invalid installation request.` error. Using an immutable identifier (e.g., sender/user id) would avoid this failure mode.
